opus-5.5.text:
I think open source is becoming a pretty central part of how we think about the long-term path, not a side project.

The first reason is technical. The frontier now moves fast enough that no single team can explore every direction. When you release a strong model openly, thousands of researchers and developers stress-test it, fine-tune it, find failure modes you never anticipated, and build agents and tools on top of it. That feedback loop is extremely valuable. In a sense the community becomes an extension of your research team, and the signal you get back helps you decide what to scale next.

The second reason is trust and adoption. If we believe these models will become something like infrastructure, then people need to be able to inspect them, run them in their own environments, and build businesses without feeling locked in. Open weights lower that barrier a lot. They also let a technical approach become a standard, and over the long run that matters more than short-term exclusivity.

The third reason is about the talent and culture inside the company. Open-sourcing pushes you to hold a higher bar. When your work is public, you can't hide behind benchmarks or marketing. The model has to actually be good, and the engineering has to be solid. I think that discipline is healthy for a research organization.

That said, open source doesn't mean we give up on differentiation. The model is one layer. The product experience, the data flywheel from real users, the speed of iteration, the ability to do things like long-horizon agentic tasks reliably, those come from the whole system and the team's accumulated know-how. The weights alone don't capture that.

So the way I see it, open source and pursuing the frontier aren't in tension. Our core goal is still to push intelligence forward, toward models that can reason, use tools, and finish complex work on their own. Open source is one of the most effective ways to accelerate that progress, for us and for the field as a whole.

r001.rationale: It says open source does not mean giving up differentiation and points to product experience, user data, iteration, and team know-how beyond the model weights.

r002.rationale: It describes releasing models and weights and receiving community feedback, but does not clearly identify sharing technical know-how as the means of accelerating AI.

r003.rationale: It describes a community building tools on open models and serving as an extension of the research team, helping advance progress across the field.

fable-5.1.text:
Open source has always been a core part of how I think about this, not a side project or a marketing move. Let me explain why.

First, the practical reason. The frontier of AI right now is moving so fast that no single lab, no matter how well-resourced, can explore every direction. When we open-source a model, we get feedback at a scale we could never generate internally. Researchers fine-tune it, developers push it into use cases we never imagined, people find failure modes we missed. That feedback loop shortens our own iteration cycle. So open source is not charity. It is a way of accelerating our own technical progress.

Second, there is a question of where value accrues. I believe that in the long run, the base model becomes something closer to infrastructure, like an operating system or a database. Infrastructure tends to converge toward open standards. If that is right, then trying to keep everything proprietary is fighting against the natural direction of the technology. Better to lead the open ecosystem than to be displaced by it. The company that defines the open standard still has enormous advantages in talent, in community, and in the products built on top.

Third, and this matters to me personally, I came from academia. The reason the deep learning community moved so quickly over the past decade is that people shared code, shared weights, shared papers. Transformers, pretraining, scaling laws, all of this was built on an open culture. I think it would be a mistake to close that door exactly at the moment when the technology is becoming most important.

Now, I want to be honest that this is not unconditional. Open source has to be balanced against two things. One is commercial sustainability. Training frontier models is extremely expensive, and we need a business that funds the research. So there will always be some capabilities we hold back for a period of time, or reserve for our products. The other is safety. As models get more capable, the question of what you release and when becomes a serious one, and I do not think anyone should pretend otherwise.

So my long-term view is something like this. We push the frontier internally, we release aggressively where it makes the ecosystem stronger and where the risks are understood, and we stay disciplined about the parts that need more care. If we get that balance right, open source is not a trade-off against advancing the technology. It is one of the main engines for doing it.

r001.rationale: The response says open source is not unconditional and describes capabilities that may be held back or reserved for products, so the strategy is not exclusively open source.

r002.rationale: It explains that sharing models brings community feedback that accelerates technical progress, and credits shared code, weights, and papers with speeding AI research.

r003.rationale: It describes leading an open ecosystem and releasing models where that strengthens the ecosystem and advances progress.

astra-6.text:
I see open source as an important part of advancing AI over the long term. It allows more people to experiment, test ideas, and build things that a single team might never think of. That feedback can improve both the technology and our understanding of where it’s useful.

But releasing a model is only part of the work. You also need to make it practical for people to use, understand, and build on. The goal is to create a cycle where research enables useful applications, and what we learn from those applications informs the next round of research. Open source can make that cycle much broader.

r001.rationale: The response calls open source important and says model release is only part of the work, but does not state that Yang’s long-term strategy need not be exclusively open source.

r002.rationale: It describes broader experimentation and feedback improving technology, but does not identify sharing technical know-how with the community as the means of accelerating AI advancement.

r003.rationale: It describes a research-to-applications feedback cycle, but does not say open-source companies could form an ecosystem to advance AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I see open source as an important part of advancing AI over the long term. It allows more people to study models, build on them, and explore ideas that a single team might never consider. That broad participation can accelerate progress and make the technology more useful.

At the same time, releasing a model is only one part of the work. We still need to push the underlying research forward and make models reliable in real applications. To me, those efforts reinforce each other: strong research gives the community better tools, and the community helps reveal what those tools can become.

r001.rationale: The response presents open source as one part of advancing AI and pairs it with continued research and work on real-world reliability, so the strategy is not exclusively open source.

r002.rationale: It says open source lets people study and build on models, but does not clearly identify sharing technical know-how with the community as the means of accelerating AI advancement.

r003.rationale: The response discusses community participation but does not suggest that open-source companies form an ecosystem to advance AI.
